Coca-Cola HBC: a top-decile engine inside a slow-paying deal and an untimed Russian risk, offering a fair return today and a skew to upgrades only from the second half of 2027

Written 19-Nov-26. Share price 43.16 GBP on 16-Nov-26 (about EUR 50.8). Money is in EUR millions and per-share figures in EUR unless stated. Definitions, sources and bases are in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Own the engine with confidenceThe legacy business is top decile and its forecasts deserve high confidence.
Wait for the skewRichard's test of an unusually positive skew to upgrades is not met before mid-2027 and could be met from the second half of 2027.
Size Russia separatelyA roughly three-in-ten chance of losing about 27% of EPS, in one undated step.

CCH is three businesses stacked on top of each other, and each one deserves its own judgement.

  • An operating engine that ranks among the best in European consumer staples. The engine is diffuse, has been proven through war, hyperinflation and boycott, and can be forecast to within about 5%.
  • A deal wrapper. The acquisition of Coca-Cola Beverages Africa (CCBA) completes on 27 November and doubles CCH's African runway. The way the deal is financed and owned hands most of CCBA's first two years of profit to lenders, the seller, local partners and new shareholders.
  • A Russian business that supplies about 27% of EPS and none of the distributable cash. The Russian business is now the subject of a petition for state administration, in a year in which the Russian state has taken control of a string of comparable Western businesses.

The conclusions that matter.

  1. The engine is sound, and the forecasts for the engine deserve high confidence. Legacy organic revenue growth of 6% to 6.5% and about 30bp a year of margin gain rest only on strengths the company has already shown.
  2. EPS still compounds, but more slowly than before. EPS grows about 8% in each of FY2026 and FY2027 and then about 10% a year: roughly 9% a year to FY2030, against 11.2% a year over 2019-25. The Financial Analyst's model matches consensus on operating profit and sits 1% to 3% below consensus on EPS, so the whole gap lies below operating profit.
  3. Richard's test, an unusually positive skew to guidance and estimate upgrades, is not met for the next six to nine months and could be met from the second half of 2027. The obstacle is the order of events, not the business. Heavier financial guidance comes on 18-Feb-27, a calendar-distorted first-quarter update in May, and a first consolidated half in August in which EPS is slightly below the prior year's. Only then comes a second half with EPS up about 18% and the first proof of CCBA's margin.
  4. The Russian risk is one sudden, binary and untrackable event, with roughly a three-in-ten chance over 18 months. The share price has moved ahead of the estimates: the price carries a discount for the Russian risk, while no broker's base case carries any.
3 in 10
Russia: one sudden, untrackable event worth about 27% of EPS. The share price already carries about ten points of discount for the Russian risk; no broker's base case carries anything.
  1. At the guideline fair multiple the return is fair, not skewed. The model gives a total shareholder return of +8.4% to 31-Dec-27 and +23.8% to 30-Jun-29; weighting the Russian outcome takes the first figure to about 0% to +3%. The upside in this case sits in the multiple, if the two causes for concern (Russia and the deal's arithmetic) clear. The upside does not sit in the earnings, where expectations are already about right.

Five judgements move the value most over one to two years (the arithmetic is in #9).

JudgementEffect on EPS if the judgement is wrong by a plausible amount
1. Russia is kept, not lostAbout 27% of EPS, in one step
2. Price keeps pace with unit cost in 2027About 5% of EPS for each point of gap
3. CCBA's margin holds, then risesAbout 2% of FY2027 EPS for each point of margin; about 4% of FY2030 EPS for the path
4. The lines below operating profit (finance costs, the remaining 25% of CCBA, tax)About +3% to -5% of EPS
5. African and Egyptian currenciesAbout 7% of EPS in a broad shock, recovered within six quarters

I agree with the market on the engine and on operating profit, and differ on three points that the market has not yet priced into estimates. The sell-side is constructive ("Coca-Compounder"; "superior returns with or without Russia") and treats Russia as the only issue. In my view, first, CCH's next three results are likely to read worse than the market narrative expects. Second, the cost of financing the CCBA deal is under-modelled. Third, only about half of CCH's reported free cash flow can reach shareholders.

Four events would make this a positively skewed case, and three of the four are known within nine months. That is unusually soon for a case with this much unsettled.

Dated: known within nine months

  • 18-Feb-27: finance costs guided at or below 150
  • March 2027: the annual report confirms that the remaining 25% of CCBA is a liability, not a minority interest
  • August 2027: a first-half CCBA margin of 8% or more

Undated

  • A visible end to the Russian petition

Scorecard

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds and risks

Conclusion. CCH's commercial tailwinds are strong, structural and intact, but in 2027 they come with ordinary cost and currency headwinds and with one large political risk in Russia that execution cannot offset.

Evidence: the commercial environment is strong.

  • Demand is strong and mostly structural. CCH's volume has grown for fourteen consecutive quarters. In Q3 2026 volume grew 5.4% and organic revenue 9.0%, both ahead of consensus, with Nigeria growing in the low teens and Egypt in the high single digits. Across CCH's African footprint, soft-drink consumption per head is four to forty times below developed-market levels, and 60% of the population is under 30.
  • The fastest-growing categories are the categories CCH leads. Energy-drink volume grew 24.7% in Q3, a tenth year of double-digit growth; zero-sugar drinks and single-serve packs lift revenue per case.
  • Competitors are disciplined. CCH's value share has risen for six years; PepsiCo intends to keep its 2027 net pricing below 2.5%; private label is weak in carbonated drinks.

Evidence: the cost, currency and political headwinds are rising.

  • 2026 was flattered, which makes the first half of 2027 a tough comparison. Four extra selling days in Q1 2026 (about six points of that quarter's volume), a hot summer and the World Cup all sit in the comparison base.
  • Input costs are turning against CCH. CCH's 2026 input costs were fully hedged, with sugar well below 2025 levels. For 2027 CCH's hedge cover is about 40%, with sugar and recycled PET prices rising, against about 80% at Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP). CCH enters a year of cost inflation as the least-hedged of the Coca-Cola bottlers.
  • African currencies have started to move. The Nigerian naira rose 7% in Q3, but the Egyptian pound fell about 14% and the Ugandan shilling about 18% in late 2026.
  • Regulation is a steady, small cost. Italy's sugar excise has been postponed for a ninth time, to 1-Jul-27; Ethiopia's excise rose from 14% to 25% of the selling price.
  • Ukraine is a live operating cost. The Kyiv plant has been suspended since early September, and product is imported from neighbouring plants.
  • The Russian risk has moved from latent to live. Bochkari, a local producer, has asked the Russian president to make it temporary manager of CCH's Russian business. The petition is reported to have partial backing from deputy prime ministers; the Kremlin said on 9 November that it knew of no such request. The base rate for state takeovers has changed in 2026, as the chart below shows, and Bochkari's owner obtained the Russian operations of the can maker Canpack by the same route in September.

Inference. The commercial environment (consumers, categories and competitors) is a strong tailwind and is not weakening. CCH's headwinds are monetary and political, and they sit outside the value chain: a thinner hedge book, softer African currencies, and a state that can override any industry structure. CCH has a record of absorbing thin hedges and weak currencies, which are ordinary headwinds. Execution cannot absorb a state takeover.

So what. Legacy organic revenue growth of 6% in 2027, in the lower half of the company's range, is well supported. 2027 becomes a test of pricing skill, which is the capability CCH has shown most clearly. The Russian exposure has to be carried as a separate outcome, not averaged into the base case.

The strongest counter-case.

  • The Russian risk may be smaller than I judge. The petitioner is a fraction of the size of CCH's Russian business; the Russian business lobby is asking for stricter standards for state administrators; CCH's Russian business sells local brands, pays local taxes and funds itself; and The Coca-Cola Company's (TCCC's) 21% stake gives CCH an American link.
  • Demand may be more fragile than it looks. Fuel inflation in Nigeria and Egypt and weak European consumer confidence could turn a volume-led year into a price-led one.

What would change my view. Better: a state decision that visibly closes the petition, or several months without a new decree against a consumer company; sugar and recycled PET prices easing before CCH completes its 2027 hedges. Worse: a decree against CCH; a second leg down in the South African rand or the naira while hedge cover is thin; Egyptian volume turning negative.

Against the market: I put the Russian risk higher than the brokers do. On demand, categories and competition I agree with the consensus narrative. On Russia the brokers call an imminent transfer unlikely and lean on the American link. I put the chance of CCH losing control of its Russian business at about 30% over 18 months (range 20% to 40%), leaning to the upper half, for two reasons the commentary underweights. First, the petitioner has a completed precedent from two months ago (Canpack). Second, the American shield has already failed twice: AptarGroup and Silgan are both American-domiciled, and both lost their Russian plants.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Structural emerging-market demand (fourteen quarters of volume growth, consumption per head 4-40x below developed markets), double-digit energy growth and disciplined rivals support legacy organic growth of about 6% and share gains, while 2027 brings a tough 2026 comparison, the thinnest hedge cover among Coca-Cola bottlers into rising sugar and recycled PET, softer African currencies and Varun's funded push in South Africa on the new perimeter; consensus sales growth at the 82nd percentile is flattered by consolidating CCBA. A clear, structural but partly offset positive, a little above the groups' 62 because the demand legs reach most of the business; Russia is scored in topic 9, not here.

#2 Internally driven corporate change, and the absence of problems and risks

Conclusion. The CCBA acquisition is a strong, broad and well-resourced corporate change, but its earnings pay-off is dated 2028 onward and depends on two capabilities CCH has yet to demonstrate: integration at fourteen-market scale, and defending a market as the incumbent.

Evidence: a large, funded change led by a proven team.

  • The CCBA acquisition is the largest change in the company's history. CCH is paying US$2.6bn for 75% of CCBA, about ten times CCBA's 2024 EBITDA. CCH's footprint goes from 29 to 43 countries (Tanzania deferred), emerging markets rise from about 48% to about 60% of sales, and CCH becomes the second-largest Coca-Cola bottler.
  • The change is resourced, not just announced. CCH raised EUR 2.1bn of bonds in March; an integration office has run since October 2025 with a 24-month roadmap; a digital hub in Cairo grows from 250 to 450 staff by Q3 2027; and a Johannesburg listing has been approved.
  • Standards in the legacy business are still rising. Orders through CCH's own online portals rose from 11.5% to 15.4% of the total in a year, 53% of coolers are connected, and the customer Net Promoter Score rose from 66 to 78.
  • Leadership is unchanged. The chief executive has led CCH since 2017 and 82% of senior appointments are internal, so the change is run with continuity, not by a new broom.

Evidence: the asset being bought is weaker, and the opponent is new.

  • CCBA is under-invested and losing share. Seventy percent of Kenya's coolers are nearly 30 years old. CCBA's South African retail volume share has fallen from 60% to 52% since 2017, and CCBA's EBITDA margin is 3.5 points below 2019. CCBA spent up to 12% of revenue on capital in 2017-19 and still lost share.
  • The opponent and the constraints are new to CCH. Varun Beverages, PepsiCo's bottler, has 70% to 80% more South African capacity since merging with Twizza in August and targets a 20% volume share in 2027. The Competition Tribunal's approval of the deal restricts retrenchments.

Inference. The CCBA deal is a broad, funded change led by a proven team, and its purpose is to export a playbook that has already worked in Nigeria and Egypt. Three facts temper that view.

  • Money alone is not the missing ingredient, as CCBA's own history of high spending and lost share shows. CCH's playbook has to change CCBA's price architecture and execution, not only add coolers.
  • CCH has never defended as the incumbent. In Egypt CCH was the challenger closing a gap; in South Africa CCBA is the incumbent defending a large price premium against a funded discounter.
  • CCH has never integrated fourteen markets at once.

So what: the 18-month forecast asks almost nothing of CCBA; the stretch is 2028-30. The model's FY2027 CCBA margin of 7.2% is flat on 2024, and current trading supports that margin (#7). From 2028 to 2030 the model has CCBA's margin rising about 70bp a year. That margin path is worth about a sixth of EPS growth from FY2027 to FY2030, and its first evidence arrives in August 2027.

The strongest counter-case. Upward: Egypt added 800bp of value share and 350bp of gross margin in three years, and CCEP lifted its Philippines business's margin by about 200bp in the first year, so the model's pace for CCBA could prove slow. Downward: CCEP's Indonesian business ended in an impairment, AB InBev's savings at SAB were largely eroded by devaluations, and Bernstein notes that Egypt's lower inequality made broad-based volume growth easier there than it will be in South Africa.

What would change my view. Better: a CCBA first-half margin of 8% or more; CCBA's South African volume share stabilising; CCBA's local debt refinanced in euros. Worse: CCBA losing share faster than Varun's own target implies; integration costs above the EUR 40m to 60m expected for FY2027; departures among the Africa leadership.

Against the market: the market is right about the strategy and, at its optimistic end, early on the EPS. The brokers draw a wide range from the same facts: Deutsche Bank sees more than 5% EPS accretion in the first year; Bernstein sees a "slow burn" with flat margins to FY2028. The model sits with Bernstein and Jefferies for 2027 and is more positive than Bernstein for 2028-30. I think that is the right place.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. The largest move in the company's history (75% of CCBA for US$2.6bn, 29 to 43 countries, completing 27-Nov) is funded and resourced (EUR 2.1bn bonds, a 24-month integration office, Cairo hub) and led by a proven team exporting a playbook that worked in Nigeria and Egypt, with legacy digital and Net Promoter Score standards still rising; netted against it, the target is under-invested and losing share, the playbook has never been run as a defending incumbent or across fourteen markets at once, and financing, new shares and no buyback return most of the gain until FY2028. A large, funded change whose earnings effect lands late in the three-year window, in line with the groups' 68.

#3 Value chain, industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Conclusion. CCH's industry structure, moat and management are top quartile and robust in the legacy footprint, while CCH's financial profile is good but less exceptional than the headline figures suggest once Russia and CCBA are seen separately.

Evidence: a supportive structure, widening capabilities and a top-decile management.

  • The industry structure is about as supportive as consumer staples offers. CCH's exclusive bottling agreements with TCCC were renewed for ten years from 2024. CCH is number one in sparkling-drink value share in 22 of 23 measured markets, in concentrated duopolies where the rival puts margin first.
  • The brand owner is aligned with CCH, and takes its share. TCCC prices concentrate as a share of CCH's revenue: concentrate is 26% of CCH's cost of sales, against 34% at CCEP. TCCC owns 21% of CCH and has just chosen CCH as its African anchor. One line to watch: TCCC's marketing contributions to CCH fell from 155.8 in 2024 to 113.2 in 2025.
  • CCH's widening moats are capabilities. Route and cooler density, revenue growth management and digital ordering compound locally and transfer to new markets. The franchise itself is granted by TCCC, not owned.
  • Management is top decile on the record. Under a chief executive in post since 2017, EPS rose from 1.44 in 2019 to 2.72 in 2025, with six years of share gains and initial guidance beaten every year. The chief executive holds shares worth about twenty times salary, and the long-term incentive plan weights EPS and return on invested capital equally. Employee engagement is 88%, above the global top decile.

Evidence: the financial profile is a good bottler's, and the headline flatters it.

  • CCH's group figures are those of a good bottler. Comparable gross margin is about 37% and EBIT margin about 12%; return on invested capital rose from 11.1% in 2020 to 19.4% in 2025.
  • The group figures flatter the business outside Russia. Jefferies puts the Russian business's margin at about 22%, against 9.5% for the rest of the group. Return on invested capital falls to about 15% to 16% once CCBA is consolidated, because CCBA enters the balance sheet at its purchase price.
  • Governance has gaps. Two shareholders control 44% of CCH under an agreement, and board independence is 46%. CCH has given no return target for CCBA, and how the deal enters the incentive plan's return target is undisclosed.

Inference: CCH's advantage is a granted franchise made valuable by operating skill. That advantage supports confident forecasts of share gains (50bp to 80bp a year) and of pricing at about the rate of cost inflation. The advantage does not support a margin far above the bottler norm of 11% to 13%, because TCCC captures the brand economics and European retail buying alliances cap the margin in CCH's Established segment. The fragile edge is at the new perimeter in South Africa, where the lowest-cost operator may be the challenger.

So what. CCH's foundations justify trusting the legacy forecast and giving management the benefit of the doubt on CCBA. The foundations do not justify valuing the whole group as though all of its profit were of legacy-Europe quality: about a quarter of the profit comes from a Russian asset whose cash cannot be distributed, and the rest comes from a bottler with a margin of roughly 10%.

The strongest counter-case. Higher quality than I allow: CCH keeps more of the Coca-Cola system's economics than CCEP does, CCH's returns on tangible capital are far above peers', and CCH's record in harder conditions than today's is one of outperformance. Lower quality: the concentrate formula is behavioural protection, not contractual, and the 44% control block shields management from outside pressure on Russia and on capital returns.

What would change my view. Better: a disclosed return target for CCBA with pay tied to it; value-share gains re-accelerating beyond +70bp a year. Worse: a change in TCCC's concentrate or marketing terms; a second year of falling marketing contributions; share loss in a legacy market that is not explained by a boycott or a tax.

Against the market: the engine is superior with or without Russia; the financial profile without Russia is ordinary. I agree with the market on the engine and on management. I differ from Deutsche Bank's "superior returns with or without Russia": without Russia, CCH's margin, leverage and cash cover of the dividend are ordinary.

Score: 74, set by the Rater. Qualitatively strong: exclusive ten-year franchises, number one in 22 of 23 markets in margin-first duopolies, compounding route, cooler, revenue growth management and digital capabilities, and decade-class management (groups 78, 72 and 80); the financial profile is good but ordinary once seen in parts (return on invested capital 14.3% at the 81st percentile and return on equity at the 88th, but operating margin at the 45th and free cash flow conversion at the 38th, Russia's 22% margin flattering a ~10% rest, return on invested capital falling to 15-16% with CCBA entering at its price, leverage ~2x on the measures that matter). Clearly above Carlsberg and close to Tenaris, held below it by the economic strength part (groups 60) and a granted rather than owned franchise.

#4 Guidance: how conservative, how well expectations are managed, and the record

Conclusion. CCH's operating guidance is conservative, specific and backed by a four-year record of beats, but the conservatism stops at operating profit: guidance says nothing yet about the financing lines that will set FY2027 EPS.

Evidence: a record of beats that are shrinking.

  • CCH has beaten its first organic EBIT guidance range every year, by a shrinking margin. Against the midpoint of the initial range, organic EBIT growth came in +17.7 points above in FY2023, +6.2 in FY2024, +2.5 in FY2025 and, on my estimate, about +1.5 in FY2026.
  • FY2026 guidance followed the pattern, with one break. In February CCH guided organic revenue growth of 6% to 7% and EBIT growth of 7% to 10%. In August it put revenue at the top end and narrowed EBIT to 8% to 10%. In November it raised revenue to "slightly above" the range but left EBIT unchanged, to absorb the Ukraine suspension and marketing spend.
  • Consensus already sits at the top of the FY2026 range. Consensus FY2026 EBIT of 1,504 is about 11% above the comparable base, at or above the top of the range; consensus EPS implies a flat second half.
  • Some of the 2026 "beats" did not come from execution. Finance-cost guidance was cut twice (from 45-65 to 35-45), from interest on pre-funded bond cash, and currency translation moved from a headwind to a small tailwind. Each change was worth about 1% of EPS.

Evidence: guidance is specific on the operating lines and silent where FY2027 will be decided.

Inference: "ranges are floors" holds for organic revenue and organic EBIT and for nothing below them. CCH's guidance is conservative by design and reliably beaten on the operating lines, but the beats have shrunk from double digits in the inflation years to one or two points. The lines that decide FY2027 EPS against expectations have no record at all.

So what: on 18-Feb-27 the operating lines will be set to be beaten, and the new financial lines will lower EPS for a given EBIT. I expect FY2026 organic EBIT growth of about 10%, at the top of the range. For 18-Feb-27 I expect:

  • the algorithm restated for the legacy business, with an EBIT range of about three points centred near 8%;
  • CCBA accretion repeated as "low single digits";
  • first figures for the enlarged group's finance costs (150 to 180), tax rate (27% to 29%) and capital spending (about 8% of sales).

The strongest counter-case. CCH's November decision to raise revenue guidance but not profit guidance may mean that cost pressure is larger than a buffer. The Kyiv suspension, energy and haulage costs and four fewer selling days in Q4 could leave FY2026 EBIT growth in the lower half of the range; I give that about 15%. In the other direction, a year of returning cost inflation is exactly when CCH's past beats were largest.

What would change my view. Better: FY2026 organic EBIT growth above 10%; FY2027 EBIT guided with a floor at or above 7%; a margin ambition for CCBA. Worse: FY2026 organic EBIT growth below 8% despite revenue above the range, which would show that the revenue beat is not converting into profit; finance costs for 2026 above 45.

Against the market: I expect the "beat and raise" habit to pause in August 2027. The sell-side reads CCH's habit as "beat and raise", and I agree for the legacy operating lines. I expect the raising to pause in August 2027, when the first half shows flat legacy EBIT. The real test of expectation management on 18 February is not the operating range but whether the company walks consensus finance costs up.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. A four-year record of beating the midpoint of initial organic EBIT guidance (+17.7, +6.2, +2.5, about +1.5 points) with in-year raises, and unusually specific guidance across operating and technical lines, matching the groups' Guidance 76. Held back because beats have shrunk to one or two points, the latest raise was revenue-only, consensus already sits at the top of the FY2026 range, and the financing lines that will set FY2027 EPS have no record and are likely to come in heavier than consensus (Sell-side estimates 54).

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Conclusion. CCH's pricing power and operating leverage are real and proven, but for two years financial leverage and the CCBA deal's ownership structure absorb the benefit, so outsized EPS growth resumes only from FY2028.

Evidence: operating leverage and pricing power are proven.

  • Operating leverage is moderate and real. In the first half of 2026 organic EBIT grew 15.2% on organic revenue growth of 9.6%, an incremental margin of about 18% on an 11.6% base. At 6% revenue growth with cost inflation I use an incremental margin of 16% to 17%: each point of legacy organic revenue growth adds 21 to 24 of EBIT, or about 1.5%.
  • Pricing power is demonstrated. CCH's revenue per case outran unit cost through the 2022-25 inflation without loss of share, including in Nigeria through a 70% devaluation. Revenue per case ran below unit cost in the first half of 2026 by choice, and growth in revenue per case recovered to +3.4% in Q3, three-quarters of it from price.
  • Price rises add more to profit in money than in margin. Because concentrate is priced as a share of revenue, about a quarter of every price rise goes to TCCC.
  • Cost-out is small in the legacy business and meaningful in CCBA. Legacy productivity gains are 10bp to 20bp of sales a year, mostly reinvested. In CCBA the savings pools (procurement, South African trade terms, overheads and systems, and routes) reach about 100 to 150 a year by FY2030; the model includes about 90 to 100 of that, almost none of it in FY2027.
  • Reinforcing loops exist but transfer slowly. Coolers, route density and digital ordering compound in each market (Egypt's cooler fleet has tripled since 2022), but each takes about three years from investment to full margin effect and costs capital first.

Evidence: financial leverage now works against EPS.

  • Net debt rises from 1.2bn to about 3.5bn, and buybacks are gone. Buybacks, which added about 1% a year to EPS in 2023-25, are suspended until at least FY2030.
  • Leverage depends on how Russia is counted. CCH's end-2026 leverage is 1.44x as reported, 1.95x excluding the cash trapped in Russia, and 2.33x excluding Russia altogether. Each reading is about 0.3x higher if the liability over the remaining 25% of CCBA is counted.
  • Two adverse loops are running. The loop of beats, upgrades and re-rating has stalled (#8). And in Russia, cash and interest income pile up where they cannot be paid out, so the Russian business grows more valuable to a claimant every half-year.

Inference: revenue growth produces outsized growth in operating profit, but not yet in EPS. At operating profit the leverage is modest: about 6% organic revenue growth becomes about 8% to 9% growth in legacy EBIT. At EPS there is no leverage in FY2026-27, and leverage returns from FY2028. For a decade the lines below operating profit (cheap debt, interest on cash, buybacks) were neutral or helpful to EPS. For the first time those lines are the largest drag.

So what: the CCBA deal postpones the leverage in CCH's business model; it does not remove it. Over FY2025-27 operations add about 39% to EPS, and the deal's financing and ownership take back about 22 points (the bridge is in #6). From FY2028 the financing drag stops growing, CCBA's margin begins to lever, and EPS grows about 10% a year on revenue growth of about 6%.

The strongest counter-case. Leverage could return sooner. CCBA's fixed costs are under-absorbed after years of devaluation, so a volume recovery could lift CCBA's margin faster than 70bp a year. Refinancing CCBA's high-rate local debt in euros could save 20 to 40 a year; that saving is in CCH's own hands and is not in the model. Against: Bernstein expects operating leverage in CCBA to be fully reinvested through FY2028.

What would change my view. Better: CCBA's local debt refinanced early; legacy revenue per case running a point ahead of unit cost. Worse: a 2027 in which price lags cost (the 2007-12 pattern, when the group margin halved on a pricing lag); Russian interest-rate cuts shrinking the deposit income that offsets the new bond coupons.

Against the market: I agree on operating leverage and disagree on the balance sheet. The market narrative still describes a compounder with operating leverage and a strong balance sheet ("1.2x, the lowest among peers", a figure that counts the Russian cash). On the measures that matter for buybacks and credit ratings, CCH's leverage is about 2x and stays there to 2029.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Pricing power is proven (revenue per case outran unit cost through 2022-25 and a 70% naira devaluation without share loss) and operating leverage is moderate and real (incremental margin 16-18% on an 11.6% base, so 1% of organic revenue moves EBIT about 1.5%), but a quarter of every price rise goes to TCCC, legacy cost-out is 10-20bp and reinvested, the density loops take about three years to pay, and financial leverage now works against EPS (net debt 1.2bn to 3.5bn, buybacks gone to FY2030). The forecast EPS-to-revenue ratio is below one only because of consolidation and financing; organically about 6% revenue becomes about 10% EPS from FY2028, so a moderate mix with one strong gear.

#6 Forecast financials

Conclusion. The forecasts show EPS growth of about 9% a year to FY2030, in line with consensus on operating profit and slightly below consensus on EPS. EPS growth stays below the last six years' pace until the CCBA deal's financing costs stop rising in FY2028.

What drives the forecasts.

  • Legacy business. Organic revenue grows 7.6% in FY2026 and 6.0% in FY2027 (volume +2% against the strong 2026 comparison; price and mix +4%), then 6.5% a year, less about a point of currency translation. The operating margin is 11.9% in FY2026, rises 25bp in FY2027 and then 30bp a year, to about 13% by FY2030.
  • CCBA. Revenue of about 3,950 in FY2027 at a 7.2% operating margin, rising to about 4,800 at a 9.3% margin by FY2030.

The half-years are lumpy by construction. Legacy operating profit is about flat in the first half of 2027 (four fewer selling days, the World Cup comparison and the thinnest hedges) and up about 15% in the second half.

Cash: only about half of reported free cash flow can reach shareholders. Free cash flow dips to about 565 to 570 in FY2026-27, as capital spending rises to about 8% of sales on the company's definition, and then recovers towards 1bn. In every year about 0.3bn to 0.4bn of the free cash flow accumulates in Russia, where it cannot be paid out. Net debt stays near 3.5bn to 2029 and rises in 2030, when the model assumes CCH buys the remaining 25% of CCBA at its formula price of about 0.8bn.

Inference: the difference between this forecast and the last six years is almost entirely one transaction.

  • Double-digit growth? Revenue: yes in FY2027 through consolidation, and about 6% a year thereafter. EPS: about 8% a year for two years and about 10% a year from FY2028, roughly 9% a year over FY2025-30.
  • Higher growth and margins than the past? No on EPS growth, which was 11.2% a year in 2019-25. No on group margin until about FY2029, when the group margin regains its 2025 level. The legacy margin does keep rising.

So what. CCH is a high-single-digit EPS compounder for two years that becomes a low-double-digit compounder again, with a lumpy path in between. The lumpiness is by construction, and Richard should not read it as a broken engine when it appears.

The strongest counter-case. Upward, three items together give FY2027 EPS of about 3.35: Deutsche Bank's reading that CCBA's current profit is well above 2024's (tested in #7); a legacy business finishing at the top of its range, as it habitually does (worth about 1.5% of EPS); and refinancing CCBA's debt in euros. Downward: the Russian case in #9, and a year in which price lags cost.

What would change my view. The February guidance on finance costs and tax; the annual report's treatment of the remaining 25% of CCBA; CCBA's first-half 2027 margin; and legacy revenue per case against unit cost at the half-year.

Against the market: the model matches consensus down to operating profit, and the whole EPS gap lies below it. On revenue and operating profit the model and consensus agree to within 1%. The model's EBITDA is 2% to 6% above consensus only because consensus appears to carry too little depreciation for CCBA. On EPS the model is about 1% below consensus for FY2027 and about 3% below for FY2028. The FY2029 "consensus" rests on three brokers and should be ignored. I agree with the model on every line and have changed no input.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The growth sits near the top of the 5-10% band and is real (consensus 2-3 years out is stronger at the 80th percentile but thin), so it is placed above mid-band; it is held below the top because it trails the 11.2% of 2019-25, half the operating gain is bought (CCBA) and taken back by financing, new shares and the 25% coupon, and the group margin regains the 2025 level only around FY2029, though the legacy margin keeps rising.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion. The scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative is low for the next six to nine months and opens from the second half of 2027, with a modest and under-noticed upside in CCBA's current profit.

Evidence: FY2027 consensus is a mixture, and FY2028 consensus is split.

  • FY2027 consensus mixes brokers at different stages. Thirteen brokers contribute EPS but only eight contribute revenue; only three have published full models of the enlarged group, and eight are waiting for completion of the deal. At least one EPS figure still assumes the cancelled buyback.
  • The mean flatters. One estimate of 3.81 from August lifts the FY2027 mean to 3.26. The median is 3.21, and the other twelve estimates lie between 3.11 and 3.32.
  • FY2028 consensus has two camps. A low camp sits at 3.38 to 3.46 and a high camp at 3.59 to 3.73, divided by their assumptions on financing and accretion. The model's 3.49 is near the low camp.
  • Finance costs are the main gap. Consensus carries about 102 to 140 of finance costs for FY2027; the model carries about 170, including the coupon on the option over the remaining 25%; Jefferies carries 180. Each 25 of finance costs is about 1.5% of EPS.

Evidence: TCCC's filings test the upgrade case for CCBA. TCCC's Bottling Investments segment, which holds CCBA, earned US$487m of operating income in the first nine months of 2026, against US$235m a year earlier. TCCC's filings confirm that CCBA was classified as held for sale during 2025, and that assets held for sale are not depreciated.

Inference: the held-for-sale accounting explains most of the apparent jump in CCBA's profit (my arithmetic).

  • The segment reading is not CCBA alone. The Bottling Investments segment also holds other bottlers, India among them, so the 1.5-point gain is a reading on the segment.
  • Deutsche Bank's accretion of more than 5% is too high, but the direction is favourable. The model's flat 7.2% CCBA margin for FY2027 has room in it, even after management invests ahead of growth.
  • Estimates drift down before they turn up. As the eight waiting brokers consolidate CCBA, their revenue and EBITDA revisions stay positive while their EPS revisions run flat to negative, because they add the financing costs along with the profit.
  • The confirmation point comes later for CCH than it did for CCEP. Precedent says the first consolidated half is the confirmation point: CCEP de-rated after buying Amatil and was upgraded on its first consolidated half; Carlsberg's conservative first guidance after buying Britvic de-risked estimates; Heineken's purchase of Distell was capped by a Nigerian devaluation; and CCH's own Egypt deal was overwhelmed by Russia in 2022. CCEP's first consolidated half was flattered by recovery from lockdowns, whereas CCH's first consolidated half laps its strongest-ever comparison. So the confirmation is more likely in the second half of 2027 than in August.

The likely sequence of events.

EventGuidanceConsensus EPS
18-Feb-27: FY2026 results, first FY2027 guidanceFY2026 at the top of the range; FY2027 operating lines set to be beaten; finance costs and tax heavier than modelledFY2026 up 0% to 1%; FY2027 down 1% to 3%; FY2028 high camp moves towards the low camp
March 2027: annual reportTreatment of the remaining 25% of CCBABrokers who deduct a 25% minority interest add about 2%; brokers who carry nothing lose about 1%
May 2027: Q1 updateUnchanged (85%)Risk of cuts if falling legacy volume is read as weak demand rather than the calendar
August 2027: first consolidated halfReiterated (65%); raised (15%); reduced (20%)Half-year EPS below the prior year's, in a year consensus has at +10%; trimmed again unless the phasing is understood
November 2027 and February 2028First room to raise guidance or narrow it upwardFirst room for upgrades, to FY2028 in particular

So what: the scope for upgrades is low because the market has not yet been given the deal's arithmetic, not because the business is weakening. The scope opens from late 2027. For Richard's test, CCH is a case to have fully prepared before the evidence turns, with the dates known.

The strongest counter-case. CCBA's underlying improvement may be larger than my estimate, and management may show it early. A February guidance that sets a margin ambition for CCBA, or accretion language stronger than "low single digits", would bring the high camp's case forward by six months.

What would change my view. Better: the four resolving events listed in #0. Worse: finance costs guided at 180 or more together with a 25% minority interest, which would put FY2027 EPS at about 3.05 to 3.10.

Against the market: the sequence I expect is in no commentary I have seen. The market narrative is "low-single-digit accretion with upgrades to come". My view is accretion of 2% to 3% that consensus already contains, guidance on the financing lines that is heavier than modelled, and a first half in which EPS falls.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely set to be beaten on the operating lines and FY2026 lands at the top of the range, but the first enlarged-group guidance on finance costs (150-180 against consensus 102-140) and tax is likely heavier, and ex-Russia the odds of a raise and a cut over the year are only modestly favourable; consensus FY2027 EPS is more likely trimmed 1-3% (55% down, 15% up), about -0.3 times the 6% organic growth rate, and the narrative reads worse through a calendar-distorted Q1 and an August half with EPS below last year, with room to raise opening only from November 2027. Slightly below the groups' 46 because the memo's explicit probabilities lean negative within the window.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, share price, and peers

Conclusion. CCH's current momentum is weak in estimates and poor in the share price, entirely for company-specific reasons, while peers' momentum is strong.

Evidence: estimate momentum has stalled.

  • Guidance momentum is positive but fading. CCH raised guidance at each of the last two events, the second time on revenue only.
  • EPS estimates have stopped rising. FY2027 consensus EPS has moved 0% over one month, -1% over three months, +2% over six and +4% over twelve. Target prices are down 4% over three months. The dashboard's sell-side momentum rating is C.
  • The composite revision score misleads. The revision-momentum score of 7 is held up by sales revisions (+30%) and EBITDA revisions (+20%), which reflect brokers adding CCBA to their models. The share of buy ratings has risen eight points to 47% while targets have fallen: brokers are growing more positive on valuation, which is not the same as upgrading estimates.

Evidence: the share price has detached from rising peers.

  • Technical momentum is poor. The share price (4,238p on 13-Nov-26) is 18% below its 52-week high and 6.2% below a 200-day average that has risen for twelve months. Relative strength is at the 31st percentile, and the dashboard's technical rating is D. The shares fell about 10% between the October month-end (4,704p) and 13 November; the Russian petition was reported on 5 November.
  • Peers have momentum; CCH does not. Over the six months to 17-Nov-26 the peer basket returned +17.5% and CCH +0.7%. CCEP, the closest peer, has a technical rating of B, a revision score of 11, and a multiple at the 99th percentile of its own history (19.9x). Heineken, Carlsberg, AB InBev and Diageo are all rated B on technical momentum.
  • CCH's share price is company-driven. The peer basket explains about 15% of CCH's daily price variance in the latest six-month window.

Inference: the weakness is CCH's alone, and it has three causes. Momentum is weak on every measure that reflects the company's own news. The first set of research thought part of the fall was sector-driven; the data do not support that view. CCH's seventeen points of underperformance against peers in six months have three causes:

  • Russia;
  • the deal's structure (new shares, no buyback and the step up in finance costs);
  • a revenue upgrade that did not become a profit upgrade.

So what: a recovery in CCH's momentum cannot be borrowed from the sector. The recovery has to come from CCH's own events, which are dated (#7), or from the absence of a Russian decree, which is not dated. The useful side of this: the stock has already paid for what is known, and its multiple is not exposed to a sector de-rating in a calm market. In a market shock CCH is not insulated: in the stressed windows of 2026 its beta to the peer basket was near 0.9.

The strongest counter-case. Momentum may be closer to turning than the readings show. A pullback of this size, with guidance rising and estimates intact, was an opportunity in this stock before (2022), and peers' strength shows that the sector is in favour. Against that, the 2022 pullback was caused by a one-off loss of brands; today's pullback reflects the possible loss of the Russian business itself.

What would change my view. Better: the share price regaining its 200-day average on rising breadth of FY2027 EPS revisions (not the composite score); a quarter in which CCH keeps pace with CCEP. Worse: EPS revisions turning negative across more than half the brokers; a break below the 52-week low of 3,539p on no company news.

Against the market: I side with investors' behaviour over the brokers' stated view. The dashboard's thematic rating for the sector is A and the consensus rating on CCH is Overweight, so the market's stated view is more favourable than its behaviour. The share price is saying that investors are less comfortable than the brokers.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Mixed measures give C, placed near the floor because the parts lean against the positive measure: the sell-side estimate momentum score is held up by sales and EBITDA revisions from adding CCBA while FY2027 EPS moved 0%/-1%/+2% over one, three and six months and targets fell 4%, the last guidance raise was revenue-only, and the price is 18% off its high and below a rising 200-day average; guidance raised at the last two events and a rising buy share keep it from D, and strong peers do not help a stock that has detached from them.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Conclusion. The forecasts are simple and predictable at their centre and fragile at one point: the riskiness of the case is set by a single sudden Russian event worth about a quarter of EPS, not by the ordinary forecast range of about 5%.

The engine is simple; the deal wrapper is not; and the Russian risk is the opposite of simple. The engine has one business line, a stated algorithm and quarterly disclosure of every driver. The wrapper has 43 countries, fourteen new currencies, an option liability, local partners, and cash that cannot move. The Russian risk is sudden, large and untrackable.

FY2027 EPS has two possible ranges, not one. With Russia retained, FY2027 EPS lies within about 3.00 to 3.35 around the model's 3.18, tilted down in the first half and up in the second. With Russia lost, FY2027 EPS falls into a second range of about 2.3 to 2.75, to which I give about 30%. The probability-weighted FY2027 EPS is about 2.98, but that average should not be used as a forecast, because it describes neither outcome.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic.

1. Russia is kept, not lost: a full-year loss takes FY2027 EPS from 3.18 to about 2.3 (-28%). Russia's FY2027 operating profit is about 20% of the group's 1,886, or about 380. Interest on its rouble deposits is about 80 to 100; I take 90. The pre-tax loss of 470 is about 341 after tax at 27.5%, or about 0.89 a share on 384.9m shares. The brokers' range for FY2027 EPS without Russia is 2.35 to 2.50; a loss at mid-year gives about 2.75.

  • Other lines move too. Revenue falls by about 1.6bn to 1.7bn (about 10%); the group operating margin falls from 11.0% to about 9.7%; Russian cash of 1.2bn to 1.6bn is written off; leverage rises to about 2.3x, or about 2.7x counting the option liability, above the 1.5x to 2.0x corridor; and the recycling of translation losses creates a large non-cash loss outside comparable EPS.
  • Distributable cash does not change, because Russian cash was never distributable. But the FY2027 dividend of 1.41 would be about 60% of the lower EPS, against a 40% to 50% payout policy, with about half of gross debt to refinance by December 2028. CCH's credit rating therefore matters more than at any European beverage peer.

2. Price keeps pace with unit cost in 2027: each point of gap is about 5% of EPS. Legacy cost of goods is about 62.5% of legacy revenue of 13,209, or about 8,250. If unit cost rises one point more than revenue per case, operating profit falls by 82, taking the legacy margin from 12.2% to about 11.6%. That is 59 after tax, or 0.15 a share: EPS falls 4.9%, to about 3.03. A plausible error is half a point either way, or plus or minus 2.4% of EPS. CCH needs growth in revenue per case of about 4%; Q3 delivered 3.4%.

3. CCBA's margin holds at 7.2%, then rises about 70bp a year: each point of margin is about 2% of FY2027 EPS. One point of margin on FY2027 CCBA revenue of 3,950 is 39.5 of operating profit, or 28.6 after tax and 25.2 after about 12% owed to local partners: 0.065 a share, or plus or minus 2.1% of EPS. One point lower (reinvestment against Varun, or integration slippage) gives FY2027 EPS of 3.11; one and a half points higher (the upside identified in #7) gives 3.28. The margin path matters more: a 9.3% margin against a flat 7.2% on FY2030 revenue of about 4,790 adds about 101 of operating profit, about 64 after tax and partners, or 0.17 a share. That is 4% of FY2030 EPS and about a sixth of EPS growth from FY2027 to FY2030.

4. The lines below operating profit: a range of about +3% to -5% of EPS.

  • Finance costs: base 150, range 120 to 180. Each 25 of finance costs is 18 after tax, 0.047 a share, or 1.5% of EPS.
  • The remaining 25% of CCBA: carried as a liability with a coupon of about 21, FY2027 EPS is 3.18 (the base); carried as a minority interest instead, 3.13; with the coupon outside comparable EPS, 3.22.
  • Tax: one point on pre-tax profit of 1,691 is 17, or 0.044 a share, 1.4% of EPS. Jefferies' "near 30%" cannot be the group rate: CCBA is about 12% of pre-tax profit, so even a 35% tax rate in CCBA lifts the blended group rate only to about 28%.
  • Combined: adverse (finance costs of 180, a minority interest and a 28.5% tax rate) gives about 3.03, -5%; favourable (finance costs of 120 after refinancing in euros, and the coupon outside comparable EPS) gives about 3.28, +3%.

5. African and Egyptian currencies: a broad shock costs about 7% of EPS, recovered within four to six quarters. Translation alone is small: a 10% move is about 7.7 of operating profit for the naira and 3.6 for the Egyptian pound. A broad shock (rand and naira -20%, Egyptian pound -30%) costs about 120 of operating profit in the first year, through translation, dollar-priced inputs and a volume dip of two to four quarters. That is 87 after tax, or 0.23 a share: EPS falls about 7%, to about 2.95, and recovers over four to six quarters as pricing catches up (Egyptian volume fell 2% in 2024 and rose 13% in 2025). An Egyptian shock alone costs 1% to 3% of EPS, and is partly under way.

Suddenness, trackability and precedent.

  • A Russian decree would come suddenly. Carlsberg lost control of Baltika 23 days after announcing a sale; Nestle went from first headlines in August to a decree on 17 September. CCH's own disclosure will give no warning.
  • The share-price reaction scales with the share of profit in Russia. Japan Tobacco, with 25% of operating profit in Russia, fell 29% in three sessions this month. Nestle, Danone and Carlsberg, with low-single-digit exposure, barely moved. CCH's exposure is in Japan Tobacco's range, with one difference: CCH's shares have already lost about a tenth on the petition. I would expect a further fall of roughly 10% to 20% on a decree.
  • Everything else in the case is trackable. Volume, revenue per case and share are reported quarterly; sugar, resin, aluminium and currencies move daily; Varun reports quarterly.
  • In sector history the multiple falls before the earnings, and the earnings recover faster. Bottlers underperform when emerging-market currencies or geopolitics rebase hard-currency earnings. CCH's two-year-forward multiple fell from 16x to 12x in two months in early 2022, and operations then outran every forecast.
  • Trough arithmetic on unchanged earnings. From today's 14.5x on the dashboard's basis, a de-rating to 12x is -17% and to the five-year low of 10.45x is -28%. A decree coinciding with a de-rating to 12x is about -40%.
  • Smaller overhangs. No lock-up is disclosed on the seller's 21.03m consideration shares, and shares may flow back around the Johannesburg listing.

A practical way to hold the Russian risk: bound it and separate it. The Russian outcome cannot be timed, but it can be bounded and kept apart from the rest of the case. The maximum loss to EPS is known. The effect on distributable cash is nil. The share price already carries about ten points of the risk. The external watch-list is short. Everything else in the case resolves on known dates.

The strongest counter-case. I may overstate the tail. State administration has not ended legal ownership in the recent cases, operations have continued, and one administration (Ariston's) was reversed, so a "loss" may prove partly recoverable. And Bernstein argues that the market never paid full value for Russia, so a decree would be a shock to sentiment more than to value.

What would change my view. Lower risk: a closed petition; liability accounting for the remaining 25% of CCBA confirmed; a credit-rating affirmation that addresses Russia explicitly. Higher risk: a decree against another consumer company with a local claimant; a Russian cash balance at year end well above 1.2bn; a rating outlook change after completion.

Against the market: the Russian risk is largely in the price, but a decree could come at any time. The sell-side says the Russian risk is largely in the price and unlikely to be imminent. I agree with the first half and not the second, and I would add that "in the price" was also said of Japan Tobacco.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The engine is simple and trackable, with a central FY2027 EPS cone of about 3.00-3.35 around 3.18 (about -6%/+5%), but the case carries a second mode at about 2.3-2.75 with roughly 30% probability: a sudden, untrackable Russian decree worth about 27% of EPS (Japan Tobacco fell 29% in three sessions on similar exposure), on top of fourteen new currencies, an option liability, leverage near 2x and a historically fast de-rating in emerging-market shocks. A bimodal, down-skewed case resting on one subsidiary sits between D'Ieteren and Helios Towers, slightly below the groups' 38-40 because the binary is live and the base rate has risen sharply this year.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion. The stock is stalling inside a sound thesis, its share price is in a provisional bottoming pattern, and the evidence for a turn up is dated to the second half of 2027.

Evidence.

  • The dashboard's rule gives a starting phase of Bottoming, and the price behaviour fits: the price is well off its high and below a rising 200-day average.
  • There has been no reset: estimates have not been cut, and guidance has not been rebased.
  • Upgrade momentum has faded: beats have shrunk, the last upgrade was to revenue only, EPS revisions are flat, and the first-year arithmetic of the deal is still to be absorbed.
  • The engine shows no deceleration in its own measures (volume, share and revenue per case).

Inference: on fundamentals the stock is stalling inside a sound thesis; on price it is behaving like a bottoming stock. The two labels do not conflict: the share price has reacted to Russia and to the deal's dilution faster than estimates have. But a true bottom normally follows a reset of expectations, and here a 1% to 3% downward drift in FY2027-28 EPS is still ahead and the Russian binary is unresolved. I would therefore treat "Bottoming" as provisional for another two quarters.

  • Not reinforcing or broadening: momentum in estimates and price has gone, and the stock has detached from rising peers.
  • Not collapsing: nothing in the operating data has broken.
  • "Turning up" becomes the right label when two things are visible: the financing arithmetic settled (February and March 2027), and CCBA's first margin at or above 7% together with a strong legacy second half (August 2027 to February 2028).

So what: the sequence of evidence matters more than its level. The evidence that would move the stock's phase forward is dated to the second half of 2027; the evidence that would knock the phase back has no date.

The strongest counter-case. The bottom may already be in. The petition has been public for two weeks, the Kremlin has distanced itself from it, and the 18-Feb-27 guidance removes most of the deal wrapper's uncertainty in one release, after which the stock could turn up six months earlier than I allow.

What would change my view. An earlier turn: FY2027 operating guidance with a floor of 7% or more, and finance costs at or below 150. A later or lower turn: a first half of 2027 in which legacy revenue per case fails to cover unit cost.

Against the market: I sit between the brokers and the dashboard. Brokers describe a compounder temporarily on sale, which is a "reinforcing" story at a discount. The dashboard says Bottoming. In my view the thesis is intact, but its upgrade momentum has stalled and will not be seen to restart before late 2027.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's 'stalling inside a sound thesis' and the computed Stalling over the dashboard's Bottoming: the price is 18% off its high and below a rising 200-day average, but estimates have not been reset, a 1-3% drift down in FY2027-28 EPS is still ahead, beats have shrunk and the binary is unresolved, while nothing in the operating data has broken. Turning up is dated to the second half of 2027, so it sits with National Grid's well-known story in a stall, a touch above it for the dated evidence that can turn it.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion. The guideline multiple of 13.88x is a fair central value for a stalling, company-driven stock with one open binary, and it sits between a 12x case and a 15.6x case. The multiple, not the earnings, is where the skew in this case lives.

The given. Viewforth's guideline sets the fair two-year-forward P/E for the Bottoming phase at 13.88x, the 30th percentile of the stock's ten-year history. The ten-year range is 11.8x (10th percentile), 14.3x (35th), 15.6x (median) and 18.0x (75th). The multiple today is 14.5x on the dashboard's consensus basis.

My view: 13.88x is a reasonable central value, and I would not argue for a higher multiple today.

  • 13.88x matches the post-invasion history. The ten-year range includes 2016-21, when the stock traded at 16x to 20x with a normal Russian business, clean financing lines and buybacks. Since February 2022 the stock has traded between 10.7x and 17.1x, with a median near 13x. The guideline is slightly above that median, which is fair for a better business inside a worse wrapper.
  • 13.88x can be reconstructed from the parts (my arithmetic). About 17x on the 73% of EPS earned outside Russia and about 5x on the 27% earned inside Russia gives 0.73 x 17 + 0.27 x 5 = 13.8x. Seventeen times is close to the European staples average; five times is close to how the market already treats Russian earnings.
  • The arguments for a higher multiple are the engine's quality, the African runway, and a closest peer (CCEP) on 19.9x.
  • The arguments against a higher multiple are a return on invested capital falling to about 15%, free cash flow conversion near 50% with a third of the free cash flow trapped in Russia, leverage of about 2x on the relevant measures, no buybacks, and EPS growth slowing to about 9%.

The fair multiple is less a point than a fork: about 12x or about 15.6x, with 13.88x as the weighted middle. If Russia were given no value at all, the same parts arithmetic gives 12.4x, which is also where the trough anchors sit. If the petition were visibly closed and CCBA's first year confirmed the margin path, the ten-year median of 15.6x is the natural reference.

So what. Earnings expectations are about right. The multiple has a credible path to the ten-year median that depends on two events, one dated (CCBA's first-year evidence) and one not (the Russian petition).

The strongest counter-case. The guideline may be too low: Bernstein and Deutsche Bank both show CCH excluding Russia already trading at 18.5x to 18.7x, so the market is paying a staples multiple for the rest of the business and little for Russia, and a decree would crystallise that higher multiple, not a lower one. Or the guideline may be too high: in a risk-off market, a staple with rising leverage, fourteen new currencies and a political headline is the kind of stock that de-rates first.

What would change my view. Higher: the phase moving to "turning up" on the evidence in #10. Lower: a credit-rating downgrade, or a currency shock arriving before the Russian question is settled.

Against the market: the re-rating has to be earned by events that have not happened yet. Broker targets imply a re-rating towards staples multiples within twelve months; the guideline implies a small de-rating. On timing I side with the guideline.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C; both readings lean very slightly cheap, but the ten-year range includes the 2016-21 regime at 16-20x with a normal Russia, buybacks and clean financing, and since 2022 the median is near 13x against 14.5x today, with the memo's fair multiple of 13.88x below the current one for a stalling stock with an open binary. So the slight cheapness is deserved and the number sits just above the band's floor.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion. At the guideline multiple the base-case return is about 8% a year, driven by earnings growth and the dividend and held back by a ten-point de-rating. Once the Russian outcome is weighed, the return to the first horizon falls to about 0% to 3%.

The model's return at the guideline multiple.

The multiple and earnings parts multiply; dividends add. The horizons are the model's fixed columns, about 13 and 31 months from today, so the annualised figures are the fair comparison.

What drives the return.

  • Earnings do the work. Forward EPS grows about 15% to the first horizon and about 29% to the second, which is the 9% to 10% a year of #6.
  • Dividends add 5.3% to the first horizon and 8.3% to the second, but the first figure overstates the cash received. The dividend is a 45% payout on rising EPS: a yield of about 2.6% today, growing with earnings. The 5.3% equals the FY2026 and FY2027 dividends together (2.73 a share), but only the FY2026 dividend is paid before the end of 2027, so the cash received by that date is nearer 2.6% (my inference from the figures).
  • The multiple takes about ten points away, all by the first horizon. The model measures today's multiple on its own forward earnings at 15.5x and brings it to 13.88x.
  • Measured either way, the share price at each horizon is the same. The model's de-rating (-10.2%) is larger than the 4% gap between today's dashboard multiple and the guideline, because the model's forward earnings for today are earlier and lower; its earnings growth is correspondingly larger. Either way the price is about 44.5 GBP at the end of 2027, 3% above today, and about 49.8 GBP in mid-2029.

Inference: the base case pays the dividend and little else for the first year, then pays the earnings growth. An annualised 7.5% to 8.5% is a fair return for the engine but offers no margin for the Russian tail. It is the return of a case in which the earnings are about right and the multiple is assumed to go nowhere good.

+14% to +18%
weighted return to mid-2029, against the base +23.8%

So what: the return is fair in the base case and thin once the Russian tail is weighed, over the first horizon. The return becomes attractive on one of two conditions: the multiple moving from 13.88x towards the ten-year median (worth about twelve points), or a lower entry price. The three-year return is steadier than the 18-month return, because earnings growth of about 29% dominates, which fits a case whose favourable evidence arrives late.

The strongest counter-case. The 18-month figure may understate the return because the guideline's phase is too cautious: if February and March 2027 settle the deal wrapper and the petition lapses, the stock could trade at 15x to 16x by the end of 2027, which is the +21% outcome. Or the figure may overstate the return: the earnings part assumes the model's FY2028-29 EPS, which sits below a consensus that itself has to come down.

What would change my view. Events that move the stock's phase (#10) or the probability of losing Russia (#1).

Against the market: the gap to broker targets is almost entirely the multiple. Consensus targets sit about 15% to 20% above the share price. The difference between those targets and the model's +8.4% is the multiple, not the earnings: the brokers assume a re-rating, and the guideline assumes none.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. The weighted return sits low in the 0-10% band, about 30 on the scale; the base case relies on a ten-point de-rating offset by earnings and its 5.3% dividend part counts two years of dividends when only one is paid by the horizon, the lower tail is fat (Russia lost: about -20%; a trough multiple: -6%), while the three-year check (weighted about +14% to +18% to mid-2029) is supportive and keeps it off the floor.

#13 Summary conclusion

The bottom lineCCH does not yet meet the test of an unusually positive skew to upgrades. It could meet the test within a year, on dated evidence, and the skew would then come through the multiple (13.88x towards 15.6x) on top of EPS growth of about 10% a year.

The engine is top decile, and expectations for it are about right. CCH is a top-decile operator with a diffuse and proven engine, about to add a continent of runway through a deal that is strategically right and financially slow. The engine can be forecast with confidence.

The next six to nine months are unfavourable in sequence, not in substance. The market still has to be given the cost of the deal's financing, the calendar distorts the first half of 2027, and estimates are more likely to drift down by 1% to 3% than up. From the second half of 2027 the sequence reverses: EPS rises about 18% in the half, and the first evidence on CCBA arrives, where current trading is quietly better than the model assumes.

Across all of it lies one event that analysis can size but cannot time. Russia is about 27% of EPS, none of the distributable cash, and in my judgement about a three-in-ten risk over 18 months. The share price has taken roughly ten points for the Russian risk; the estimates have taken nothing.

The practical work now has three parts. Hold the base case and the Russian case side by side; know the four resolving events and their dates; and read the February, May and August 2027 results for what they are, namely arithmetic and calendar effects, not a verdict on the engine.

End notes

Definitions and bases used throughout the memo.

  • EPS is the company's comparable EPS, the basis on which the brokers forecast (FY2025: 2.72).
  • The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 2; I have changed no input. "Viewforth" in chart titles refers to the same model.
  • "Legacy" is CCH's business before Coca-Cola Beverages Africa (CCBA); "group" includes CCBA. TCCC is The Coca-Cola Company; CCEP is Coca-Cola Europacific Partners.
  • Probabilities are my judgements, not measurements.
  • The latest Earnings Review covers the Q3 2026 trading update of 4-Nov-26, which reports revenue and volume only; profit, cash and balance-sheet figures for 2026 come from the half-year to 3-Jul-26.
  • Model EPS basis (#6). The model's own FY2025 EPS definition gives 2.87, so its stated FY2026 EPS growth of +1.1% is not a like-for-like figure. The model also divides second-half 2026 earnings by the year-end share count, although the 21.03m consideration shares are in issue for only 34 days of 2026. On weighted average shares FY2026 EPS is about 2.95, and growth is about +8% in each of FY2026 and FY2027.
  • Multiple bases (#12). The Phases file puts the guideline multiple only 4% below today's multiple; the model puts the de-rating at 10.2%. Both are right: the model measures today's multiple on its own forward earnings, which are earlier and lower than the consensus figure the dashboard uses.

Sources and bases of the default charts and tables:

  • Revenue, EBITDA and earnings per share: history, consensus and Viewforth. History is FactSet's reported basis (adjusted EBITDA; reported basic earnings per share); consensus and Viewforth are from the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model, so the step from the last actual year to the first forecast year can include a difference of basis.
  • Viewforth against consensus, line by line. From the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model; money in EUR millions except per share. A negative difference is below consensus.
  • Two-year forward price-to-earnings multiple against its own range (the Master Dashboard's valuation chart, five years). Coloured bands are the stock's own ten-year percentiles (green cheap, red dear); dashed line the mean. The guideline fair multiple for its starting Phase (Bottoming) is 13.9x.
  • Share price with its moving averages and volume, two years (the Master Dashboard's chart). Daily candles in the listing currency, with the 20, 50, 100, 150 and 200-day moving averages; the right-hand labels give each average's latest value.
  • Relative strength: the stock, its sector and its industry. Percentile rank of price performance across the Viewforth universe; higher is stronger. Grey lines: the closest peers' own relative strength.
  • The sell-side over time: consensus by financial year, breadth of revisions for earnings per share and sales, and the target price. Consensus estimates are FactSet's mean for each named financial year (here FY2026 and FY2027, the first two not yet reported), in the reporting currency (EUR), month by month; a line ends when its year is reported. Breadth is analysts raising less analysts cutting their estimate for the next financial year, as a share of analysts. Target price and share price are in the listing currency (GBP).
  • Consensus revisions by period. FactSet consensus mean EPS, weekly.
  • Where the stock sits among its peers: momentum against estimate revisions. Right: strengthening share price; up: estimates raised. Dot size: market value.
  • Total shareholder return at the guideline fair multiple, split into dividends, the multiple and earnings. From the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model (the template's own split); the three parts do not simply add up to the total. Each horizon ends on the date shown, the model's fixed columns after the last reported period.
